source.title: Relating Adversarially Robust Generalization to Flat Minima
source.authors: David Stutz; Matthias Hein; B. Schiele

record.file_problem: Full paper text, including supplementary material, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests flatness against adversarial robustness and robust overfitting. Those are distinct from the claim's natural-label generalization behavior; no listed version covers these results.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own results on adversarial robust generalization and flatness. These are recorded under fits_no_version because the claim and its versions concern natural-label generalization.
record.test_reason: Although the main analysis concerns adversarial robustness, Table 5 also reports clean held-out classification error for optimizer, batch-size and dropout comparisons. These results bear on V4, V5 and V6 in the new setting of adversarially trained CIFAR-10 ResNet-18 models. The robust-loss flatness results do not test V7's standard generalization-gap claim.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that adversarial robustness is associated with flatter robust-loss landscapes, and that several flatness-oriented or regularizing methods improve robustness. This is principally correlational evidence and does not establish the standard generalization-gap relationship in V7.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses adversarial training and measures adversarial robust loss and robustness, rather than the standard natural-label training and test error in the source claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Flatness/generalization association depends on the measure: average-case flatness in RLoss is more strongly associated with robustness than worst-case flatness (reported correlation 0.54), clean-loss average flatness is less predictive (0.27), and worst-case flatness is more sensitive to the neighborhood size ξ. Robust overfitting is also affected by hyperparameters and training method.

fits_no_version.finding: Average-case robust-loss flatness correlates with robust test loss at Pearson/Spearman 0.85/0.87; worst-case flatness has Pearson correlation 0.54.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Relative weight-perturbation flatness in robust loss tracks adversarial held-out loss across the evaluated models, with a stronger association for average-case flatness.

fits_no_version.finding: Average-case clean-loss flatness correlates with robust test loss at only 0.27.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The association between flatness and adversarial robustness depends on which loss defines flatness.

fits_no_version.finding: Training robust loss continues falling while test robust loss rises; flatter models generally have smaller robust loss gaps and less robust overfitting.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Robust-loss flatness tracks adversarial overfitting and the adversarial train-test loss gap.

fits_no_version.finding: The clean-loss maximum Hessian eigenvalue changes from 1990 to 505 or 7936 under scaling that preserves robustness.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The unnormalized maximum Hessian eigenvalue is not a scale-invariant predictor of adversarial robustness.

fits_no_version.finding: The proposed relative flatness measures remain approximately invariant under the tested convolutional weight and bias scaling.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Per-layer relative perturbation neighborhoods make the tested robust-loss flatness measures approximately invariant to these rescalings.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE International Conference on Computer Vision
record.problems: The evidence is confined to adversarially trained CIFAR10 models and adversarial robustness. Flatness measures require choices of perturbation neighborhood size; worst-case flatness is more sensitive to ξ. Evaluation is restricted to the first 1000 test examples, and the main analysis treats RLoss as a proxy for robust generalization while noting its disconnect from robust test error in some regimes.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. Extensive per-method, hyperparameter, and early-stopping results concern adversarial training and adversarial robustness; retained rows capture the paper's main reported relationships and measurement qualifications rather than enumerate every plotted configuration.

Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity.

Longer training or recipe adaptations to recover large-batch performance, and language benchmarks.
Dropout configuration sweeps, very small training sets, excessive dropout and jointly removing dropout and weight decay under augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness ranking standard train-test error gaps among similarly fitted models, including comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.

record.verdict_notes: The record's blanket exclusion of clean generalization overlooks the clean Err columns in Table 5. Existing rows remain outside the listed versions; the V4–V6 verdicts rely on missing table results. No listed original-source exclusion applies.

Convolutional versus fully connected architectures on natural-label image classification.

rows.subject: AT baseline (ResNet-18)
rows.operation_detail: Measured average-case flatness in robust loss and its correlation with robust generalization across trained models.
rows.measure: Pearson/Spearman correlation between average-case flatness and robustness measured by RLoss
rows.locator: Section 4.2, Improved Robustness Through Flatness; Figure 8
rows.note: The correlation concerns adversarial robustness and robust loss, not natural-label generalization.
rows.check: The reported 0.85/0.87 correlations are across evaluated models and methods, not the AT baseline alone. They relate robust test loss to robust-loss flatness, not standard train-test error gaps.

rows.subject: AT baseline (ResNet-18)
rows.operation_detail: Measured worst-case flatness in robust loss against robust generalization across trained models.
rows.measure: Pearson correlation between worst-case flatness and robust generalization
rows.locator: Section 4.2, Improved Robustness Through Flatness; Figure 8
rows.note: Authors describe this relationship as less clear than for average-case flatness.
rows.check: The 0.54 correlation is across evaluated models, not the baseline alone, and concerns robust test loss rather than the standard generalization gap.

rows.subject: AT baseline (ResNet-18)
rows.operation_detail: Compared flatness measured on clean loss with robust loss and robust generalization.
rows.measure: Pearson correlation between RLoss and average-case flatness in clean Loss
rows.locator: Supplementary Section D, Flatness of Clean Loss Landscape
rows.note: Authors say correctly measuring flatness in RLoss is crucial to establish the reported relationship.
rows.check: The 0.27 correlation is across evaluated models. Measuring clean-loss flatness does not make the outcome standard generalization: the correlated outcome remains robust test loss.

rows.subject: AT baseline (ResNet-18)
rows.operation_detail: Tracked robust loss on training and test examples over training epochs.
rows.measure: Training and test robust loss over epochs
rows.value: Training RLoss continuously decreases while test RLoss eventually increases; test RLoss and RErr start increasing shortly after the first learning-rate drop at epoch 60.
rows.note: This is adversarial robust overfitting, not natural-label training versus test error.
rows.check: The training trajectory correctly records robust overfitting, but does not measure any listed version's effect.

rows.subject: AT baseline (ResNet-18)
rows.operation_detail: Compared test and training robust loss and the effect of early stopping across methods.
rows.measure: Association of robust generalization gap with flatness
rows.value: The text states that robust methods generally reduce the test−train RLoss gap and that flatter minima generally correspond to smaller gaps.
rows.locator: Figure 9 and Section 4.2, Decomposing Robust Generalization
rows.note: The paper's gap is defined for adversarial robust loss.
rows.check: Figure 9 compares multiple methods and early-stopping conditions, not only the baseline. Its gap is test-minus-train robust loss, outside V7's standard error-gap comparison.

rows.subject: AT baseline (ResNet-18)
rows.operation_detail: Compared maximum Hessian eigenvalue with adversarial robustness across model settings.

conditions.value: maximum Hessian eigenvalue of clean loss

rows.measure: Association of maximum Hessian eigenvalue with adversarial robustness
rows.value: The text states that the largest eigenvalue is not correlated with adversarial robustness; baseline maximum eigenvalue is 1990, scaling up gives 505, and scaling down gives 7936 without affecting robustness.
rows.note: This result concerns a clean-loss geometry measure and adversarial robustness.
rows.check: The scaling values are correct, but the cross-model non-correlation concerns adversarial robustness and an unnormalized Hessian measure, not V7's magnitude-aware sharpness and standard generalization gap.

rows.subject: AT (baseline), scaled ×0.5, scaled ×2
rows.operation_detail: Scaled convolutional-layer weights and biases, then measured robust loss and flatness.
rows.measure: Effect of scaling on predictions, robust loss landscape and flatness measures
rows.value: Scaling has negligible impact on the RLoss landscape; reported flatness measures remain nearly invariant.
rows.uncertainty: Differences attributed to randomness in computing the measures.
rows.note: The authors state that batch normalization essentially cancels the scaling effect on predictions.
rows.check: The scaling experiment establishes approximate invariance of the proposed robust-loss flatness measures; it does not establish their association with the standard generalization gap.
